module

public import Mathlib.Data.Matrix.Basic

@[expose] public section

variable {n : ℕ}

open Finset

/--
A latin square of order `n` is an `n × n` matrix with entries in `Fin n` such that each symbol
appears exactly once in every row and exactly once in every column.
-/
structure LatinSquare (n : ℕ) where
  mat : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) (Fin n)
  /-- Each row is a permutation of `Fin n`. -/
  row_injective : ∀ i, Function.Injective (mat i)
  /-- Each column is a permutation of `Fin n`. -/
  col_injective : ∀ j, Function.Injective (mat.transpose j)

set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false in
/--
There are finitely many latin squares of order `n`, since each is determined by a matrix in
the finite type `Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) (Fin n)`. This is useful for defining the maximum number of
transversals over all latin squares of order `n`.
-/
instance : Fintype (LatinSquare n) :=
  Fintype.ofEquiv
    {mat : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) (Fin n) //
      (∀ i, Function.Injective (mat i)) ∧ (∀ j, Function.Injective (mat.transpose j))}
    { toFun     := fun ⟨mat, h⟩ => ⟨mat, h.1, h.2⟩
      invFun    := fun L => ⟨L.mat, L.row_injective, L.col_injective⟩
      left_inv  := fun _ => rfl
      right_inv := fun _ => rfl }

/--
A transversal of a latin square `L` is a selection of one cell per row, given by a
column-selector `σ`, such that the selected columns are all distinct and the symbols at the
selected cells are all distinct.
-/
abbrev IsTransversal (L : LatinSquare n) (σ : Fin n → Fin n) : Prop :=
  Function.Injective σ ∧ Function.Injective (fun i => L.mat i (σ i))

/--
A near-transversal of a latin square `L` of order `n` is a selection of `n - 1` cells,
given by a row-selector `ρ` and a column-selector `σ` (both `Fin (n - 1) → Fin n`),
such that the selected rows are all distinct, the selected columns are all distinct,
and the symbols at the selected cells are all distinct.
-/
abbrev IsNearTransversal (L : LatinSquare n) (ρ σ : Fin (n - 1) → Fin n) : Prop :=
  Function.Injective ρ ∧ Function.Injective σ ∧ Function.Injective (fun i => L.mat (ρ i) (σ i))

/--
The number of transversals of a latin square `L`, defined as the cardinality of the type of
column-selectors `σ : Fin n → Fin n` satisfying `IsTransversal L σ`.
-/
def numTransversals (L : LatinSquare n) : ℕ := Fintype.card {σ : Fin n → Fin n // IsTransversal L σ}

status_issues.recorded: FormalConjectures/Paper/LatinSquare.lean records @[category research open] and answer(sorry).
status_issues.source_status: Proved affirmatively by Eberhard–Manners–Mrazović (2015 preprint; published in J. Eur. Math. Soc. 21 (2019), 441–463).
status_issues.evidence: https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.05987, introduction and Theorem 1.2: “In this paper we prove Vardi's conjecture with the optimal values c₁,c₂ = 1/e + o(1), thus also confirming Wanless's conjecture.” Their count satisfies s_n = n! z_n and s_n = (e^(-1/2) + o(1)) n!³ / n^(n-1) for odd n. This gives the exponential bounds; finitely many smaller odd n ≥ 3 can be absorbed into the constants because 0 < z_n < n!. Publication confirmed at https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/841.
status_issues.suggested_change: Change the category to research solved and answer(sorry) to answer(True); add the Eberhard–Manners–Mrazović reference.

status_issues.recorded: FormalConjectures/Paper/LatinSquare.lean records @[category research open], answer(sorry), and the remark that existence of the limit is not known.
status_issues.source_status: Proved affirmatively by Eberhard–Manners–Mrazović (2015 preprint; published in J. Eur. Math. Soc. 21 (2019), 441–463).
status_issues.evidence: https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.05987, introduction, explicitly restates Wanless's limit as (1/n) log(s_n/n!²) → -1 and says their result confirms it. Since the same introduction identifies s_n/n! with the number z_n of cyclic Latin-square transversals, this is exactly the Lean limit along odd orders. Their Theorem 1.2 proves the stronger asymptotic z_n = (e^(-1/2) + o(1)) n!² / n^(n-1).
status_issues.suggested_change: Change the category to research solved and the answer to answer(True). Replace the obsolete limit-existence remark with the result and its reference.

reformulations.difference: The structure requires injective rows and columns rather than explicitly requiring each symbol to occur exactly once.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every row and column is an endofunction of the finite type Fin n. Such a function is injective iff it is bijective, equivalently iff every symbol has exactly one preimage. Matrix.transpose interchanges the indices, so the column condition is correct. Proved the full matrix-condition equivalence in scratch.lean, including n = 0.

reformulations.difference: Wanless defines a transversal as an unlabelled set of n cells with distinct rows, columns and symbols; Lean represents it by a column selector.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The graph of σ contains exactly one cell in each row and hence n cells. The two injectivity conditions give distinct columns and symbols. Conversely, a standard transversal has a unique cell in every row, determining a unique σ. Proved the graph characterization and existence equivalence with finite cell sets in scratch.lean.

reformulations.difference: Lean represents a near-transversal by two functions indexed by Fin (n - 1), rather than an unlabelled set of n - 1 cells.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The image of i ↦ (ρ i, σ i) has n - 1 cells because ρ is injective, and the three injectivity conditions give precisely the source's coordinate and symbol restrictions. Conversely, enumerate any standard near-transversal by Fin (n - 1) and project its coordinates. Proved both the selector characterization and the existential equivalence. Multiple enumerations do not affect its existential use. Also proved that including order zero in the universal near-transversal statement adds only a true case.

reformulations.difference: The definition counts valid column-selector functions instead of sets of cells.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The selector-to-graph correspondence is a bijection, not an n!-to-one enumeration: the row coordinate uniquely determines the index of each selected cell. The theorem number_counts_cell_sets in scratch.lean proves equality with the cardinality of the type of standard transversal cell sets, so no normalization factor or symmetry quotient is missing.

review.notes: Checked all five declaration groups, including the structure fields and instFintypeLatinSquare, and their sole problem-file user. No conflicting Mathlib Latin-square definition was found. The finite maximum T is attained for every order; MOLS families cannot repeat a square when n ≥ 2. Lean computations gave Latin-square counts [1,1,2,12] for orders 0–3 and cyclic transversal counts [1,1,0,3,0,15] for orders 0–5. Empty and singleton cases agree with the stated conventions. /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles without errors or warnings, and its equivalence/counting proofs have no sorryAx dependency. Additional use-site checks are in uses.lean. The reviewed file remains byte-identical to the committed version. The OEIS entry page was unavailable, but its numeric b-file was read and corroborated against the survey.
